strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated, systematic study of conditioning for diffusion-based representations in control: it first demonstrates empirically (Fig. 1, Fig. 3a) that text conditions—a strategy that works in perception tasks—fail or hurt in control tasks, then diagnoses the failure through cross-attention analysis showing poor text-to-region grounding in control environments (Fig. 3b,c). This negative result and analysis is a genuinely useful contribution to the community.

The proposed ORCA method is simple and well-aligned with the diagnosis: learnable task prompts (implicit task grounding) plus frame-wise dense visual prompts from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, learned end-to-end with a standard behavior cloning loss, requiring no diffusion model fine-tuning.

Evaluation is reasonably broad and convincing: 12 tasks across three established benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) following the VC-1 protocol, with strong margins over task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (CoOp, TADP) baselines, and with the same compression-layer setup applied to all baselines for fairness (Table 1-3).

Ablations support the design choices: component analysis (Table 4) shows complementary gains from task and visual prompts; layer-selection study (Table 5) and timestep ablation (Table 6) are informative; efficiency analysis (Table 7) honestly reports the added latency and parameter count.

Qualitative analyses (attention visualizations in Fig. 3 and Fig. 6, including dynamic frame-wise attention shifts in Relocate) provide intuitive evidence that the learned prompts attend to task-relevant regions and behaviors, and the appendix provides reproducibility details (compression layer pseudocode, full text conditions, baseline descriptions).
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the core components are established techniques—CoOp-style learnable prompt tokens (Zhou et al., 2022), visual prompting of diffusion features (SD4Match, EcoDepth), and diffusion features for control (SCR, Gupta et al., 2024). The contribution is largely the observation that these must be adapted for control, plus a straightforward combination; there is no fundamentally new mechanism.

Key clarifying ablations are missing. Most notably, there is no ablation testing how much the diffusion pre-training itself matters (e.g., same architecture with random initialization), given that t=0 is used—effectively a nearly noise-free forward pass—leaving open whether ORCA is truly leveraging diffusion representations or simply an over-parameterized conditioned feature extractor. A comparison to fine-tuning a strong encoder (e.g., DINOv2 with a comparable parameter budget), which the introduction argues against, would also strengthen the case.

Notational and textual errors undermine precision: in Eq. 3 the condition is written C* = τθ(p_t; p_v) but then described with 'task prompt p_v and visual prompt p_v' (variable names swapped/duplicated, and p_t is used for both task and visual prompts earlier in the same sentence); the BC loss is written in terms of εθ(z_t,t;C*) while the text says intermediate feature maps are used. These should be corrected.

The improvements, while consistent, are modest on some benchmarks (e.g., MetaWorld mean 95.2 vs. 93.1 for TADP; DMC 74.3 vs. 70.7), with high variance on some tasks (Cheetah-run ±8.4, Adroit VC-1 Pen ±16.7) and only three seeds; on Adroit Relocate, ORCA merely matches CLIP (44.0). Statistical significance is not discussed.

Evaluation is limited to simulated benchmarks with very few demonstrations (2-5); no real-robot experiments or generalization tests (e.g., to visual distractors or unseen scenes) are provided, so the practical value of the 'task-adaptive' claim beyond the benchmark suite remains unverified.

Computational overhead is significant relative to frozen-encoder baselines (48ms vs. 11ms for VC-1, ~1.6x parameters), and the paper does not discuss whether this cost is justified in deployment contexts.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated question: how to condition pre-trained diffusion models for robotic control, and provides an honest, negative empirical finding (§4.1) that text conditions—which work well in perception tasks (Zhao et al., 2023; Kondapaneni et al., 2024)—can degrade control performance, supported by cross-attention map analysis (Fig. 3b,c).

The proposed method is simple and well-executed: learnable task prompts plus dense visual prompts from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, trained end-to-end with a standard behavior cloning objective, requiring only ~10.6M learnable parameters (Table 7).

Comprehensive evaluation across three benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit; 12 tasks), consistently outperforming both task-agnostic baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and adapted task-adaptive baselines (Text, CoOp, TADP) in Tables 1–3.

Thorough ablation studies covering component contributions (Table 4), U-Net layer selection (Table 5), diffusion timesteps (Table 6), efficiency (Table 7), and null-condition attention analysis (Fig. 7), plus qualitative rollouts in Appendix C.
weaknesses: Notational and consistency errors undermine confidence: Eq. 3 defines the condition as τθ(pt; pv) using 'pv' for both task and visual prompts, and the text states 'task prompt pv and visual prompt pv'—the task prompt should be pt. Such sloppiness in the core formulation is concerning.

There is an unexplained numerical inconsistency: the timestep ablation (Table 6) reports the default t=0 configuration at mean 70.8 (e.g., Reacher-easy 71.9 ± 5.6), whereas Table 1 reports the same ORCA configuration at mean 74.3 (Reacher-easy 87.6 ± 2.9). No explanation reconciles these numbers, casting doubt on reproducibility of the headline result.

Absolute gains over the strongest task-agnostic baseline (SCR, also Stable Diffusion) are modest and high-variance: DMC 74.3 vs 68.3, with Cheetah-run showing ±8.4 to ±11.3 standard deviations across ablations. With only 3 seeds, several claimed improvements may not be statistically robust (e.g., Adroit Relocate 44.0 for both SCR† and ORCA).
Latency is nearly 4.4× that of VC-1 (48ms vs 11ms, Table 7), a material practical drawback for real-time control that is not discussed in terms of deployment implications.

Conceptual novelty is incremental: learnable prompt tokens (CoOp, Textual Inversion) and dense visual features as conditions (SD4Match, EcoDepth) are established techniques; the contribution is primarily their application and empirical validation in control, rather than a new methodological idea.

Evaluation is simulation-only (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) with very few demonstrations (2–5); no real-robot experiments or out-of-distribution generalization tests are provided, limiting evidence that the task-adaptive conditioning transfers beyond the training distribution.

Framing concern: since task prompts are learned per task with full downstream supervision, 'task-adaptive' amounts to task-specific optimization of a subset of parameters; the paper does not test multi-task settings or whether learned prompts transfer across related tasks, which would strengthen the core claim.

Minor presentation issues: mixed citation of CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) vs OpenCLIP (Cherti et al., 2023) in Appendix C, and the hypothesis in §4.2 that conditions should vary per frame is only weakly validated—the visual prompts are frame-dependent, but no experiment directly isolates frame-wise vs static visual conditioning.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and relatively underexplored question: how to condition frozen text-to-image diffusion models for robotic control, and convincingly demonstrates that the standard recipe from perception tasks (VLM-generated text conditions) transfers poorly. The cross-attention map analysis (Fig. 3b,c; Fig. 6; appendix A.3) provides a genuine diagnostic insight — in domain-mismatched tasks like Cheetah-run, text tokens fail to ground to the agent, explaining why captions can even hurt performance relative to the null condition.

The proposed method (ORCA) is simple and sensible: learnable task prompts replace fragile text descriptions, and dense DINOv2 features projected through a small conv layer serve as frame-wise visual prompts, all learned end-to-end with a standard behavior cloning objective. The design is justified by the preceding analysis rather than appearing arbitrary.

Evaluation is reasonably broad and careful: 12 tasks across three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit), three seeds with standard deviations, and a strong baseline set that includes both task-agnostic representations (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and adapted task-adaptive prompting methods (Text Simple/Caption, CoOp, TADP). ORCA improves the mean on all three suites (74.3 vs 70.7 TADP on DMC; 95.2 vs 93.1 on MetaWorld; 65.3 vs 58.0 on Adroit).

Useful ablations covering component contributions (Table 4), diffusion layer selection (Table 5), timestep choice (Table 6), parameter/latency overhead (Table 7), and a null-condition analysis (A.3). Notably, the authors are transparent that ORCA is ~4x slower than VC-1 (48ms vs 11ms) and that individual task/visual prompts show divergent per-task behavior.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear motivation → analysis → method → validation narrative.
weaknesses: A critical control experiment is missing: a DINOv2-only baseline (dense DINOv2 features passed through the same compression layer directly to the policy, without the diffusion model). Since ORCA's visual prompts carry DINOv2 features, part of the gain could stem from DINOv2 rather than from diffusion conditioning itself. The paper shows SCR (SD, null condition) = 68.3 vs ORCA = 74.3 on DMC, which suggests conditions help, but without a DINOv2-only reference it is hard to attribute the improvement cleanly to 'task-adaptive diffusion conditioning.'

Discrepancies between reported numbers raise reproducibility concerns: e.g., the default t=0 configuration in Table 6 reports Reacher-easy 71.9±5.6 and DMC mean 70.8, while Table 1 reports 87.6±2.9 and mean 74.3 for what should be the same configuration (Walker-stand and Cheetah-run also differ slightly). Additionally, Fig. 1 shows ORCA MetaWorld = 96.3 while Table 2 reports 95.2. These inconsistencies need explanation.

Layer selection (down_1-3, mid) is chosen based on downstream evaluation performance on the same benchmarks used for the final comparison, which constitutes a mild form of benchmark-specific tuning that could overstate generalization.

Evaluation is entirely in simulation; no real-robot experiments or out-of-distribution generalization tests. The domain-gap argument (web images vs. simulated control environments) is central to the paper's hypothesis, yet the method's behavior on real-world imagery — where text conditions should presumably work better — is untested, leaving the domain-gap explanation partly unvalidated.

Novelty is moderate: the method combines established techniques (learnable prompt tokens à la CoOp/Textual Inversion, external dense vision-encoder features à la SD4Match/EcoDepth) and applies them to control; the main novelty lies in the analysis and the adaptation rather than a new mechanism.

Computational overhead is substantial (480M params, 48ms vs 11ms for VC-1) and diffusion-feature extraction is required per frame; the paper does not discuss implications for real-time control or larger observation histories.

Minor presentation issues: notation errors in Section 6.4/Eq. 3 (task prompt 'p_v' and visual prompt 'p_v' confused; 'train both ... task prompts pt and visual prompts pt'), inconsistent typographic details in Table 2 ('± 2,3'), and success rates are reported as best among online evaluation trials, which can flatter results compared to final-episode success.

strengths: The paper poses a clear and well-motivated question: how should text-to-image diffusion models be conditioned for robotic control, given that text conditioning—successful in other vision tasks—fails here. The motivating analysis (Fig. 3 cross-attention maps showing that text tokens fail to ground in control environments like Cheetah-run) is an insightful and well-executed diagnostic study that goes beyond simply reporting numbers.

The proposed method (ORCA) is simple, well-motivated, and end-to-end trainable with a standard behavior cloning objective: learnable task prompts replace text prompts, and dense visual prompts from an auxiliary vision encoder capture frame-specific details. The design is clearly justified by the preceding analysis.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 tasks across three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) following the VC-1 protocol, plus LIBERO-Long for long-horizon and multi-task settings. ORCA consistently outperforms task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (Text Simple/Caption, CoOp, TADP) baselines, establishing state-of-the-art on all suites (e.g., mean 74.3 on DMC vs 70.7 for the best baseline; 95.2 on MetaWorld vs 93.1; 65.3 on Adroit vs 58.0).

Thoughtful ablations: component analysis of task vs visual prompts, layer selection in the U-Net, timestep ablation, vision encoder choice, and comparison against full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (Table 3 shows fine-tuning collapses performance while ORCA uses only 10.6M learnable parameters). The efficiency analysis (Table F) transparently reports the added latency and parameter count.

Good reproducibility: implementation details are thorough, including full text prompts used for baselines (Table G), pseudo-code for the compression layer, and backbones/settings; the appendix also honestly addresses limitations (U-Net-based SD 1.5 only) and negative results with SVD and SD 3.0.
weaknesses: A confound in attributing the gains to 'conditioning the diffusion model': the visual prompts are dense DINOv2 features injected via cross-attention. This is essentially a mechanism for fusing extra dense visual features into the encoder, and part of the improvement may come from this additional information rather than from task-adaptive conditioning of the diffusion representation per se. Table 4 shows task prompts alone yield only modest gains (69.8 vs 68.3 for the null condition on DMC mean), and the paper would benefit from a stronger control, e.g., injecting DINOv2 dense features directly into the policy/feature stream without the diffusion model.

All evaluation is in simulation; there is no real-robot experiment. Given the paper's claims about domain gap being a central issue for text conditioning, validating on real-world control data would substantially strengthen the argument.
Latency increases from 11ms (VC-1) to 48ms per observation (Table F), which is significant for control; the practical implications for closed-loop control are not discussed in depth.

Some per-task improvements are within one standard deviation (e.g., Finger-spin 68.0±1.0 vs 66.6±2.7 for SCR; Walker-stand 89.1±1.8 vs 89.0±2.9 for TADP), so the consistent-improvement claim, while supported by means, relies on averages over only three seeds in a high-variance imitation learning setting.

Novelty is moderate: learnable prompt tuning (CoOp, Textual Inversion) and conditioning diffusion features for perception (VPD, TADP, SD4Match) are established; the contribution is primarily a careful adaptation and empirical study for robotic control rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Presentation issues: the 'Visualization of task and visual prompts' paragraph on page 8 is duplicated verbatim; there are minor typos ('directlyt', 'as of in TADP', 'their effectiveness is limited as shown by their minimal gains'); Table 3's LoRA row appears to use a different PEFT method for SCR while RoboAdapter is used for VC-1, making the fine-tuning comparison slightly asymmetric.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated question: whether the conditioning mechanisms that make diffusion features successful in perception tasks (e.g., VPD, TADP) transfer to robotic control, and it answers this with a systematic progression from text conditions to learned task/visual prompts.

The experimental evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: 12 tasks across DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit following the VC-1 protocol, 3 seeds with standard deviations, plus LIBERO-Long results showing applicability to long-horizon and multi-task settings.

The baseline set is thoughtful—beyond CLIP/VC-1/SCR, the authors adapt prompting methods from perception (CoOp, TADP, Textual Inversion) to control, which directly tests their hypothesis rather than only comparing to generic encoders.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: cross-attention grounding studies (Fig. 3), analysis of <bos>/<eos> attention behavior for the null condition, layer-wise feature selection (Table 5), timestep ablations, backbone comparisons (SVD, SD 3.0), and fine-tuning comparisons (Table 3) collectively support the design choices.

The comparison with downstream fine-tuning (Table 3) convincingly demonstrates that prompt learning avoids the catastrophic overfitting of full fine-tuning (SCR collapsing to 9.3) while adding only ~10.6M learnable parameters.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. ORCA is essentially the composition of existing components—learnable soft prompt tokens (CoOp/Textual Inversion-style), dense features from an off-the-shelf vision encoder (DINOv2) projected through a convolutional layer, and frozen diffusion features from early U-Net blocks (already used by SCR). The paper's contribution is the application and the empirical study rather than a new technique.

A key ablation isolating the conditioning mechanism is missing. The visual prompts are DINOv2 features injected via cross-attention; a baseline where DINOv2 features are simply concatenated with the diffusion features as policy input (bypassing the conditioning pathway entirely) would clarify whether the gains come from conditioning diffusion representations or merely from having access to DINOv2 information. Table C shows even SD-VAE features as prompts help, suggesting the mechanism may matter less than the paper claims.

The narrative that 'text conditions yield minimal or even negative gains' is somewhat overstated by the presented evidence. Table 1 shows Text (Caption) beats the null/SCR baseline on nearly all DMC and MetaWorld tasks (e.g., 92.5 vs 90.4 mean on MetaWorld); the negative case is concentrated in Cheetah-run and Adroit Relocate. The figure-level framing (Fig. 1, Fig. 3a) emphasizes failures that the tables show to be mixed.

There are notable presentation and correctness issues: Eq. 3 uses 'pt' for both task and visual prompts and mislabels pv twice in the surrounding text; Section 6.5 contains a fully duplicated paragraph ('Visualization of task and visual prompts' appears twice verbatim); the pseudocode in Algorithm 1 applies BatchNorm2d(hidden_dim) after a conv producing compress_dim channels, which is dimensionally inconsistent as written; and there are multiple typos ('directlyt', 'each tasks', 'provide provide'). These indicate insufficient care in the final manuscript.

Practical cost is significant and somewhat downplayed: 480M parameters and 48ms latency versus 11ms for VC-1 (Table F) is a 4x inference-time overhead, which matters for a control setting, yet this is discussed only briefly in the appendix.

Evaluation is confined to simulation with very few demonstrations (2–5 per task), so the claimed state-of-the-art on 'robotic control' has not been tested on real-robot data or in higher-variance regimes where task-adaptive conditioning might behave differently.

Standard deviations in some tables are large relative to the reported gains (e.g., Cheetah-run ±8.4, down_2 layer ±18.8 on Reacher), and with only 3 seeds the improvements on individual tasks are not always statistically compelling, even if the aggregate trend is consistent.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated question—how to condition frozen text-to-image diffusion models for robotic control—and the diagnosis is convincing: the cross-attention analysis in Fig. 3 (well-grounded attention for Button-press vs. noisy grounding for Cheetah-run, plus the null-condition analysis in A.7) provides concrete, interpretable evidence for why text conditions transfer poorly from web-image domains to control environments.

The proposed ORCA is simple and clearly specified: learnable task prompts shared across observations plus dense frame-wise visual prompts from a vision encoder, trained end-to-end with a standard behavior cloning objective, without modifying the diffusion model. The design directly follows from the empirical observations.

Evaluation is broad and thorough: 12 tasks across DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit following the VC-1 protocol, plus LIBERO-Long (including multi-task training) in the appendix. ORCA consistently outperforms task-agnostic baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and adapted task-adaptive baselines (CoOp, TADP), establishing state-of-the-art on all suites.

The ablations substantiate each design choice: component analysis (Table 4), layer selection (Table 5), timestep selection (Table D), choice of vision encoder (Table C), and different diffusion backbones (Table A). The fine-tuning comparison (Table 3) is valuable, showing that full fine-tuning of SCR collapses while ORCA achieves better results with modest learnable parameters.
The efficiency analysis (Table F) is transparent about costs (480M total params, 48ms vs. 11ms for VC-1), and limitations are honestly discussed (Section C).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Both components are adapted from prior work—learnable text tokens (CoOp/Textual Inversion [70, 11]) and prompt-style conditioning via an external encoder (SD4Match, EcoDepth [33, 43])—applied to a new domain. The contribution is best viewed as a careful empirical study rather than a fundamentally new technique.

There is a possible confound in the central claim: the 'task-adaptive representation' is obtained partly by injecting frozen DINOv2 features into the condition. ORCA thus effectively ensembles two strong pre-trained encoders (SD U-Net + DINOv2), and some of the gains may come from the added DINOv2 features rather than from 'conditioning' per se. While Table C (w/o vision encoder: 54.7 vs. 65.3) and Table E (DINOv2 alone: 52.5) show the combination outperforms each part, a baseline that concatenates diffusion and DINOv2 features directly into the policy (bypassing cross-attention conditioning) would more cleanly isolate the benefit of the conditioning mechanism.

The headline finding that text conditions yield 'minimal or even negative gains' is somewhat in tension with the full results: in Table 1, Text (Caption) achieves 92.5 on MetaWorld (vs. SCR's 90.4) and 68.9 on DMC, i.e., text conditions actually help in many tasks. The negative-gain claim mainly rests on Cheetah-run and a few Adroit tasks; the framing in Fig. 1 and the abstract slightly overstates the failure mode.

Evaluation is simulation-only (MuJoCo-based benchmarks) with very few demonstrations (2–5 per task); no real-robot experiments are provided, which limits evidence of practical usefulness. The task subsets are also small (5+5+2), so per-task variability (e.g., Cheetah-run's 50.0 ± 8.4) is non-trivial.

Minor presentation flaws that should be corrected: a duplicated paragraph on page 8 ('Visualization of task and visual prompts' appears twice verbatim), a notation error in Eq. 3 where both prompts are written as p_t (p_v intended), the loss is written with a plain norm '||...||' without specifying the norm order, and C* = τθ(p_t; p_v) is loosely defined. No explicit statement of code release is given, which affects reproducibility of the full pipeline (Gemini prompt, layer selection, hyperparameters).
Inference latency nearly quadruples relative to VC-1 (48ms vs. 11ms), which is disclosed but may matter for real-time control; the trade-off discussion is brief.
